    Basis vectors 𝐛1,𝐛2,𝐛3\mathbf{b}_{1},\mathbf{b}_{2},\mathbf{b}_{3} of reciprocal lattice

  • 𝐤\mathbf{k}

    Reciprocal space vector either in 𝐤∈3\mathbf{k}\in\real^{3} or a reciprocal lattice 𝐤∈Γ∗\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}

  • 𝐥\mathbf{l}

    Lattice vector 𝐥∈Γ\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma

  • 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega}

    Unit cell

  • 𝐫\mathbf{r}

    General position vector (element of 𝐫∈3\mathbf{r}\in\real^{3})

  • 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}

    Position vector of atom ii

  • Γ\Gamma

    Lattice

  • Γ∗\Gamma^{*}

    Reciprocal Lattice

  • f^\hat{f}

    Fourier transform of function ff

  • Ω\Omega

    Volume of Unit cell

  • ff

    Generic function (potentially in a suitable function space)

  • kk

    Standard norm (2-norm) or magnitude of vector 𝐤\mathbf{k}

  • rr

    Standard norm (2-norm) or magnitude of vector 𝐫\mathbf{r}

  • ri​jr_{ij}

    Distance between atoms ii and jj

S1 Mathematical Conventions, Notation and Prerequisites

Many different conventions and notations can be found in the literature for mathematical expressions and concepts. Most relevant to this work are the ones relating to periodic lattices and Fourier transforms. To keep a consistent notation and convention throughout this document, we summarize all definitions in this section. We also briefly summarize some well-known mathematical results about these that are used throughout this document and the implementation.

S1.1 Vectors, Norms and Inner Products

Throughout this document, we shall use the bold-font 𝐫∈3\mathbf{r}\in\real^{3} for vectors in Euclidean space, while r=‖𝐫‖r=\|\mathbf{r}\| will denote its magnitude computed using the usual 2-norm. Similarly, we will use 𝐤∈3\mathbf{k}\in\real^{3} and k=‖𝐤‖k=\|\mathbf{k}\| when discussing Fourier transforms, and write either 𝐤⋅𝐫\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r} or just 𝐤𝐫\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r} for the inner product between two vectors.

For an atomic system consisting of N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} atoms, we index the atoms by i,j∈{1,2,…,N}i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,N\}. This is then used to write 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} for the position vector of atom ii, and ri​j=‖𝐫j−𝐫i‖r_{ij}=\|\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{r}_{i}\| for the distance between atoms ii and jj.

For the more mathematically inclined readers: 𝐫\mathbf{r} and 𝐤\mathbf{k} technically are elements of different vector spaces, both isomorphic to 3, which are duals of each other. In practice, the choice of symbol will unambiguously determine which space is meant.

S1.2 Lattice and Reciprocal Lattice

The lattice Γ\Gamma spanned by the three linearly independent vectors 𝐚1,𝐚2,𝐚3∈3\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2},\mathbf{a}_{3}\in\real^{3} is defined as

Γ\displaystyle\Gamma =spanℤ​{𝐚1,𝐚2,𝐚3}\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{Z}}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2},\mathbf{a}_{3}\} (S1)
={𝒍=n1𝐚1+n2𝐚2+n3𝐚3|n1,n2,n3∈ℤ}.\displaystyle=\{\boldsymbol{l}=n_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+n_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}+n_{3}\mathbf{a}_{3}|n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}\}. (S2)

In practice, these basis vectors will be chosen to specify the periodicity within the cell. We can then define the reciprocal lattice Γ∗\Gamma^{*} by the requirement

Γ∗={𝐤∈3|∀𝐫∈Γ:𝐤𝐫∈2πℤ}\displaystyle\Gamma^{*}=\{\mathbf{k}\in\real^{3}|\forall\mathbf{r}\in\Gamma:\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}\} (S3)

which can be shown to be the lattice spanned by the three basis vectors

𝐛i=2​π​𝐚j×𝐚k𝐚i⋅(𝐚j×𝐚k),\displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{i}=2\pi\frac{\mathbf{a}_{j}\times\mathbf{a}_{k}}{\mathbf{a}_{i}\cdot(\mathbf{a}_{j}\times\mathbf{a}_{k})}, (S4)

where (i,j,k)(i,j,k) is an even permutation of (1,2,3)(1,2,3) and ×\times is the cross-product. We will generally use the symbol 𝒍∈Γ\boldsymbol{l}\in\Gamma to denote an element of the (real space) lattice, i.e. a different symbol from 𝐫\mathbf{r}, while we use the same symbol 𝐤∈Γ∗\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}. It should be clear from context which one is meant. In particular, we will write

∑𝐤\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{k}} (S5)

as a shorthand for

∑𝐤∈Γ∗\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}} (S6)

as the former is likely to be more familiar to be many readers. The summation symbol is emphasizing that 𝐤\mathbf{k} only runs over the discrete set Γ∗\Gamma^{*} rather than 3.

Note that we do include the factor of 2​π2\pi directly in the definition of the reciprocal space vectors, since this leads to slightly more compact formulae and also is slightly more convenient for implementations.

S1.3 Unit cells and volumes

In practice, the basis vectors 𝐚1,𝐚2,𝐚3\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2},\mathbf{a}_{3} introduced in the previous subsection will be used to specify a periodic repetition of atoms. In this case, the volume of the unit cell spanned by the three vectors can be obtained by computing their triple product, and will be denoted by

Ω=𝐚1⋅(𝐚2×𝐚3).\displaystyle\Omega=\mathbf{a}_{1}\cdot(\mathbf{a}_{2}\times\mathbf{a}_{3}). (S7)

In order to compute Fourier transforms, it will also be necessary to integrate over such a unit cell. We can thus define the closed set

𝛀={w1𝐚1+w2𝐚2+w3𝐚3|w1,w2,w3∈[0,1]}\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\{w_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+w_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}+w_{3}\mathbf{a}_{3}|w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}\in[0,1]\} (S8)

for the unit cell, such that its volume Ω=Vol⁡(𝛀)\Omega=\mathrm{Vol}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}).

For the mathematically inclined readers: strictly speaking, it would be more correct to define 𝛀=3/Γ\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\real^{3}/\Gamma using a quotient, where Γ\Gamma is the lattice defined by the basis vectors. With this definition, the periodic structure of the underlying domain becomes more explicit, and it is easy to see that 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega} is diffeomorphic to the 3-torus 𝕋3=S1×S1×S1\mathbb{T}^{3}=S^{1}\times S^{1}\times S^{1} as a smooth manifold.

S1.4 Fourier Series and Fourier Transforms

In this chapter, we shall make extensive use of the Fourier transform in its various forms.

Firstly, consider functions f:3→ℂf:\real^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} (or more precisely, absolutely integrable functions f∈L1(3,ℂ)f\in L^{1}(\real^{3},\mathbb{C})). Then, for all 𝐤∈3\mathbf{k}\in\real^{3}, we define the Fourier transform of ff as

f^(𝐤)=∫3d3re−i​𝐤𝐫f(𝐫).\displaystyle\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})=\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}^{3}r\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}f(\mathbf{r}). (S9)

The inverse transformation then is given by

f(𝐫)=1(2​π)3∫3d3kei​𝐤𝐫f^(𝐤).\displaystyle f(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}^{3}k\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}\hat{f}(\mathbf{k}). (S10)

The entire factor of 1(2​π)3\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}} is thus contained in the inverse transform. While this is arguably less elegant from the point of view of symmetry, it will lead to slightly simpler expressions when comparing this to the Fourier series for periodic functions, which will be helpful when discussing the Poisson summation formula.

If the original function ff is rotationally symmetric, often written as f⁡(𝐫)=f⁡(r)f(\mathbf{r})=f(r), then so is its Fourier transform f^​(𝐤)=f^​(k)\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})=\hat{f}(k). By doing the integral in spherical coordinates and integrating with respect to the angular variables (ϕ,θ)(\phi,\theta), we can obtain the more direct formula relating ff to f^\hat{f} as the one-dimensional integral

f^​(k)\displaystyle\hat{f}(k) =4​π​∫0∞d​r​r2​sin⁡(k​r)k​r​f​(r)\displaystyle=4\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}r\,r^{2}\frac{\sin(kr)}{kr}f(r) (S11)
=4​πk​∫0∞d​r​r​sin⁡(k​r)​f​(r)\displaystyle=\frac{4\pi}{k}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}r\,r\sin(kr)f(r) (S12)

and its inverse

f⁡(r)\displaystyle f(r) =1(2​π)3​4​πr​∫0∞d​k​k​sin⁡(k​r)​f^​(k).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{4\pi}{r}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}k\,k\sin(kr)\hat{f}(k). (S13)

In particular, this means that apart from a factor of 1(2​π)3\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}, the radially symmetric transform is its own inverse. This version of the transform is closely related to the Hankel transform.

So far, we have discussed the Fourier transform of a generic (absolutely integrable) function on 3. We now move on to the Fourier series representation of a periodic function.

Let f:3→ℂf:\real^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} be a function having the periodicity of a unit cell 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega} with its corresponding lattice Γ\Gamma. More mathematically, this means that for all 𝐫∈3\mathbf{r}\in\real^{3} and 𝐥∈Γ\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma, f⁡(𝐫+𝐥)=f⁡(𝐫)f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l})=f(\mathbf{r}). The function is clearly specified by just its values in the unit cell 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega}.

For any reciprocal space vector 𝐤∈Γ∗\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}, we then define the Fourier transform (for the periodic case also called Fourier series coefficient) of ff as

f^​(𝐤)=∫𝛀d3​r​e−i​𝐤𝐫​f​(𝐫).\displaystyle\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})=\int_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\mathrm{d}^{3}r\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}f(\mathbf{r}). (S14)

We can then recover ff using the inverse transform

f⁡(𝐫)=1Ω​∑𝐤∈Γ∗f^​(𝐤)​ei​𝐤𝐫.\displaystyle f(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}}\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})e^{i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}. (S15)

Note that a common convention is to put the factor of 1/Ω1/\Omega in the (forwards) Fourier transform rather than the inverse. Our convention makes the expressions for the forward transforms for the aperiodic case in Equation S9 and periodic one in Equation S14 more symmetric.

S1.5 The Poisson Summation Formula

The following theorem provides us with an explicit connection between summation in real space and reciprocal space.

Theorem S1.1 (Poisson Summation Formula).

Let f∈L1(3,ℂ)f\in L^{1}(\real^{3},\mathbb{C}) be an absolutely integrable function, Γ\Gamma a lattice whose unit cell 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega} has a volume Ω\Omega and Γ∗\Gamma^{*} its reciprocal lattice. Then, for all 𝐫∈3\mathbf{r}\in\real^{3}, we get

∑𝐥∈Γf⁡(𝐫+𝐥)=1Ω​∑𝐤∈Γ∗f^​(𝐤)​ei​𝐤𝐫.\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l})=\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}}\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})e^{i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}. (S16)

In other words, a sum of the values of ff over a lattice Γ\Gamma can be expressed as a sum over reciprocal space vectors.

While this is a standard result in mathematical methods, it is so important to our work that we provide a short proof for the convenience of the reader. There is no originality in the proof, and this is merely to make this document more self-contained.

Proof.

Let F⁡(𝐫)=∑𝐥∈Γf⁡(𝐫+𝐥)F(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}) be the left-hand side. We will first show that FF is a periodic function with respect to the lattice Γ\Gamma. From the inversion of Fourier transforms for periodic functions, this then means that we can write FF using its Fourier series coefficients F^​(𝐤)\hat{F}(\mathbf{k}) as

F⁡(𝐫)=1Ω​∑𝐤∈Γ∗F^​(𝐤)​ei​𝐤𝐫.\displaystyle F(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}}\hat{F}(\mathbf{k})e^{i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}. (S17)

Comparing this with the theorem, we can see that all we need to do is to show that F^​(𝐤)=f^​(𝐤)\hat{F}(\mathbf{k})=\hat{f}(\mathbf{k}) for all 𝐤∈Γ∗\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}.

Starting with the periodicity of FF, this comes from the fact that for two lattice vectors 𝐥,𝐥′∈Γ\mathbf{l},\mathbf{l}^{\prime}\in\Gamma, their sum is still just a lattice vector 𝐥′′=𝐥+𝐥′∈Γ\mathbf{l}^{\prime\prime}=\mathbf{l}+\mathbf{l}^{\prime}\in\Gamma. A sum over all 𝐥′∈Γ\mathbf{l}^{\prime}\in\Gamma is equivalent to a sum over all 𝐥′′=𝐥+𝐥′\mathbf{l}^{\prime\prime}=\mathbf{l}+\mathbf{l}^{\prime}, since we are effectively just shifting the origin of the lattice by 𝐥\mathbf{l}. Thus,

F⁡(𝐫+𝐥)\displaystyle F(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}) =∑𝐥′∈Γf⁡(𝐫+𝐥+𝐥′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{l}^{\prime}\in\Gamma}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}+\mathbf{l}^{\prime}) (S18)
=∑𝐥′′∈Γf⁡(𝐫+𝐥′′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{l}^{\prime\prime}\in\Gamma}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}^{\prime\prime}) (S19)
=F⁡(𝐫).\displaystyle=F(\mathbf{r}). (S20)

We can thus compute the Fourier transform of FF (the variant for periodic functions, also called Fourier series) directly from the definition in Equation S14. For 𝐤∈Γ∗\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}, we get

F^​(𝐤)\displaystyle\hat{F}(\mathbf{k}) =∫𝛀d3​r​e−i​𝐤𝐫​F​(𝐫)\displaystyle=\int_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\mathrm{d}^{3}r\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}F(\mathbf{r}) (S21)
=∫𝛀d3​r​e−i​𝐤𝐫​∑𝐥∈Γf⁡(𝐫+𝐥)\displaystyle=\int_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\mathrm{d}^{3}r\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}) (S22)
=F​u​b​i​n​i​∑𝐥∈Γ∫𝛀d3​r​e−i​𝐤𝐫​f​(𝐫+𝐥)\displaystyle\overset{Fubini}{=}\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}\int_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\mathrm{d}^{3}r\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}) (S23)
=𝐤𝐥=2​π​n​∑𝐥∈Γ∫𝛀d3​r​e−i​𝐤​(𝐫+𝐥)​f​(𝐫+𝐥)\displaystyle\overset{\mathbf{k}\mathbf{l}=2\pi n}{=}\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}\int_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\mathrm{d}^{3}r\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l})}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}) (S24)
=𝐫′=𝐫+𝐥∫3d3r′e−i​𝐤𝐫′f(𝐫′)\displaystyle\overset{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}=\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}}{=}\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}^{3}r^{\prime}\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}f(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) (S25)
=f^​(𝐤).\displaystyle=\hat{f}(\mathbf{k}). (S26)

This shows that the Fourier series coefficients F^​(𝐤)\hat{F}(\mathbf{k}) of the periodic function FF are actually identical to the Fourier transform of the (in general, aperiodic) function ff. The only key difference is that f^​(𝐤)\hat{f}(\mathbf{k}) is defined for all 𝐤∈3\mathbf{k}\in\real^{3}, while F^​(𝐤)\hat{F}(\mathbf{k}) only is defined for 𝐤∈Γ∗\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}. Thus, F^\hat{F} is merely the restriction of f^\hat{f} onto the reciprocal lattice Γ∗\Gamma^{*}.

We can now use the inverse transform for FF, which allows us to write

F⁡(𝐫)=1Ω​∑𝐤∈Γ∗F^​(𝐤)​ei​𝐤𝐫.\displaystyle F(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}}\hat{F}(\mathbf{k})e^{i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}. (S27)

But since F^​(𝐤)=f^​(𝐤)\hat{F}(\mathbf{k})=\hat{f}(\mathbf{k}), this leads to

F⁡(𝐫)=1Ω​∑𝐤∈Γ∗f^​(𝐤)​ei​𝐤𝐫.\displaystyle F(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\Gamma^{*}}\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})e^{i\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}}. (S28)

Remembering that we had defined F⁡(𝐫)=∑𝐥f⁡(𝐫+𝐥)F(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{l}}f(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{l}), this concludes the theorem. ∎

S2 Derivation of Ewald Summation

S2.1 General Expression using Poisson Summation

In this section, we derive the general decomposition of the potential into its four terms in the Ewald summation. For an explanation of the notation and terminology related to unit cells, periodic lattices and Fourier transforms, please refer to the previous section.

The results in this section are already known in the literature. The purpose of this section is to make this paper self-contained, and to include derivations of all results using a consistent notation that we also use in the main text.

S2.2 Self-Term in Ewald Summation

The self-term in Ewald summation can be obtained by computing the limit

vself\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{self}} =limr→0vLR​(r).\displaystyle=\lim_{r\rightarrow 0}v_{\mathrm{LR}}(r). (S29)

To evaluate this, we can use the Taylor series expansion of the lower incomplete Gamma function, which can be derived directly from its definition and using Fubini’s theorem to interchange the order of summation and integration for a>0a>0:

γ⁡(a,x)\displaystyle\gamma(a,x) =∫0xd​t​ta−1​e−t\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{x}\mathrm{d}t\,t^{a-1}e^{-t} (S30)
=∫0xd​t​ta−1​∑n=0∞(−1)nn!​tn\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{x}\mathrm{d}t\,t^{a-1}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}t^{n} (S31)
=∑n=0∞(−1)nn!​∫0xd​t​tn+a−1\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}\int_{0}^{x}\mathrm{d}t\,t^{n+a-1} (S32)
=∑n=0∞(−1)nn!​1a+n​xa+n\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}\frac{1}{a+n}x^{a+n} (S33)
=1a​xa+𝒪⁡(xa+1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{a}x^{a}+\mathcal{O}\left(x^{a+1}\right)\,. (S34)

Using this, we obtain

vself\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{self}} =limr→01Γ⁡(p2)​γ⁡(p2,r22​σ2)rp\displaystyle=\lim_{r\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)}\frac{\gamma\left(\frac{p}{2},\frac{r^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}{r^{p}} (S35)
=1Γ⁡(p2)​2p​(2​σ2)−p2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)}\frac{2}{p}(2\sigma^{2})^{-\frac{p}{2}} (S36)
=1Γ⁡(p2+1)​(2​σ2)p2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Gamma\left(\frac{p}{2}+1\right)(2\sigma^{2})^{\frac{p}{2}}} (S37)

S2.3 Charge Neutralization term in Ewald Sum

The correction term to enforce charge neutrality arises from the interaction of the particles with a homogeneous background charge density that is used to neutralize the system.

For this, consider the Green’s function G⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)G(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) describing the potential at position 𝐫\mathbf{r}, assuming the presence of a particle at 𝐫′\mathbf{r}^{\prime} with weight (or charge) q=1q=1, including its periodic images and a homogeneous background with total charge −q-q per unit cell to fulfill charge neutrality. Then,

G⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle G(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) =∑𝐥∈Γv(𝐫−𝐫′+𝐥)−1Ω∫3d𝐫′v(𝐫−𝐫′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}v(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}+\mathbf{l})-\frac{1}{\Omega}\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\,v(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) (S38)
=∑𝐥∈ΓvSR(𝐫−𝐫′+𝐥)+∑𝐥∈ΓvLR(𝐫−𝐫′+𝐥)−1Ω∫3d𝐫′v(𝐫−𝐫′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}v_{\mathrm{SR}}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}+\mathbf{l})+\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}v_{\mathrm{LR}}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}+\mathbf{l})-\frac{1}{\Omega}\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\,v(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}) (S39)
=∑𝐥∈ΓvSR(𝐫−𝐫′+𝐥)+1Ω∑𝐤≠0v^LR(𝐤)ei​𝐤​(𝐫−𝐫′)−1Ω∫3d𝐫′vSR(𝐫−𝐫′),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\Gamma}v_{\mathrm{SR}}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}+\mathbf{l})+\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\neq 0}\hat{v}_{\mathrm{LR}}(\mathbf{k})e^{i\mathbf{k}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})}-\frac{1}{\Omega}\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\,v_{\mathrm{SR}}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}), (S40)

where the Poisson summation formula was used in the last step. The first two terms simply correspond (once summing over neighbor atoms jj) to the real and reciprocal space sums in Ewald summation. The last term is the desired correction term, which represents an additional term in the potential due to the homogeneous background charge.

To evaluate this last term, we define the convenient shorthand

vcharge\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{charge}} =∫3d𝐫vSR(𝐫).\displaystyle=\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\,v_{\mathrm{SR}}(\mathbf{r}). (S41)

The integrand is just written as vSR​(𝐫)v_{\mathrm{SR}}(\mathbf{r}) instead of vSR​(𝐫−𝐫′)v_{\mathrm{SR}}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}), as the integral runs over the entire space anyway. The actual charge correction term due to an atom with charge qq, with its compensating background charge being spread over volume Ω\Omega and taking into account an additional factor of 1/2\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} from double counting thus gives

Vi,charge=−12​qΩ.\displaystyle V_{i,\mathrm{charge}}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{q}{\Omega}. (S42)

The calculation of the charge correction term has now been reduced to the computation of

vcharge\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{charge}} =∫3d𝐫vSR(r)\displaystyle=\int_{\real{}^{3}}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\,v_{\mathrm{SR}}(r) (S43)
=4​π​∫0∞d​r​r2​vSR​(r),\displaystyle=4\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}r\,r^{2}v_{\mathrm{SR}}(r), (S44)

where we used spherical symmetry in the last step.

While we could directly start computing this for the general case, it is instructive to first study the behavior at the two bounds of the integral, i.e. what happens in the limits as r→0r\rightarrow 0 and r→∞r\rightarrow\infty. Firstly, since vSR​(r)v_{\mathrm{SR}}(r) was explicitly constructed to decay quickly as r→∞r\rightarrow\infty, the upper bound of integration does not cause any problems. On the other hand, we know that vSRv_{\mathrm{SR}} contains the singularity of the bare 1/rp1/r^{p} potential as r→0r\rightarrow 0. To estimate the lower bound of integration, we can thus study the simplified integral

∫0Rd​r​r2​1rp\displaystyle\int_{0}^{R}\mathrm{d}r\,r^{2}\frac{1}{r^{p}} =∫0Rd​r​r2−p,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{R}\mathrm{d}r\,r^{2-p}, (S45)
={13−p​r3−p|0Rp≠3log⁡p|0Rp=3\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{3-p}r^{3-p}\Big|_{0}^{R}&p\neq 3\\ \log p\Big|_{0}^{R}&p=3\end{cases} (S46)
=limϵ→0{13−p​R3−p−ϵ3−pp<3log⁡R−log⁡ϵp=3−1p−3​1Rp−3+1p−3​1ϵp−3p>3\displaystyle=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\begin{cases}\frac{1}{3-p}R^{3-p}-\epsilon^{3-p}&p<3\\ \log R-\log\epsilon&p=3\\ -\frac{1}{p-3}\frac{1}{R^{p-3}}+\frac{1}{p-3}\frac{1}{\epsilon^{p-3}}&p>3\\ \end{cases} (S47)

S2.4 Treatment of Charge Compensation Term

Summarizing the results on the compensation term and the subtlety regarding the critical exponent of p=3p=3:

  1. 1.

    For p≤3p\leq 3, the sums used to compute the potential are divergent if the cell is not charge neutral, thus requiring the addition of a homogeneous charge density of opposite total charge to ensure a neutral cell. The potential of some particle ii then consists of contributions from the remaining particles (including periodic images), and a second term Vi,chargeV_{i,\mathrm{charge}} arising from the interaction of the particle with the homogeneous background. Using a compensating background for p>3p>3 is not necessary, and as we show below, it is in fact not possible, as such a term would diverge.

  2. 2.

    This additional interaction Vi,chargeV_{i,\mathrm{charge}} has been computed explicitly in the previous subsection, and can be seen to be finite for p<3p<3 and divergent for p≥3p\geq 3. Thus, one approach is to use a compensating background for p<3p<3 and to properly take into account the additional interaction with the background charge using Vi,chargeV_{i,\mathrm{charge}}, while not to use any background at all for p>3p>3, and hence also Vi,chargeV_{i,\mathrm{charge}}.

  3. 3.

    For the critical case p=3p=3, charge neutrality does need to be enforced, but due to the divergence of the interaction between a potential compensating background, it is not possible to account for this. We thus set Vi,charge=0V_{i,\mathrm{charge}}=0, which essentially means that for this special case, we are not fully taking into account the interaction between the background and the particles.

  4. 4.

    To be more consistent and ensure continuity of the potentials as the exponent pp is varied, it would be an option to also set Vi,charge=0V_{i,\mathrm{charge}}=0 for p<3p<3. While this is a possibility, we decided against this as for the most important case of the Coulomb potential, it is common to include this term. We have therefore prioritized consistency with other Ewald implementations for p=1p=1. It should be easy for power users to change this to any other desired convention.

S3 Relation to LODE and Evolution of Method

We now discuss in some detail the relation between this work and some of our previous work for long-range ML, in which we have introduced the Long-Distance Equivariant (LODE) descriptors 1 and extensions thereof 2. While the framework presented in this work does also support LODE, we recommend in most cases to use the simpler (exterior) potential features. As we will now show, the majority of the long-ranged information of a system is contained in these features. For more complicated cases, however, there might be benefits to using the full LODE features.

The central tool that has driven these developments is a mathematical theorem called multipole expansion, which is discussed in detail in the supporting information of our previous work 2.

The first half of this section discusses some of the key ideas that led from the original formulation 1 to previous work published in 2023 2. The second half then discusses the more recent developments that led to this work.

S3.1 First Two Mathematical Consequences: From Original to Previous Work

We begin by discussing some of the inefficiencies in the original formulation of LODE 1, which have already been addressed in a previous publication 2. We provide this background because our newer developments are continuations of these improvements, and also to provide a more transparent description of why we decided to seemingly change direction.

The LODE features (assuming a single chemical species for simplicity) are parametrized by three indices (n,ℓ,m)(n,\ell,m), n=0,1,…,nmax−1n=0,1,\dots,n_{\mathrm{max}}-1, ℓ=0,1,…,ℓmax\ell=0,1,\dots,\ell_{\mathrm{max}} and for each ℓ\ell, mm takes the usual (2​ℓ+1)(2\ell+1) distinct values m∈{−ℓ,−ℓ+1,…,ℓ}m\in\{-\ell,-\ell+1,\dots,\ell\}. Hence, for fixed ℓmax,nmax\ell_{\mathrm{max}},n_{\mathrm{max}}, the total number of LODE features is given by

nmax⋅(ℓmax+1)2.\displaystyle n_{\mathrm{max}}\cdot(\ell_{\mathrm{max}}+1)^{2}. (S58)

This number is directly proportional to the computational cost that is required to generate the features – although when using a reciprocal-space implementation there is a large constant overhead associated with the global Fourier transform operations that might be dominant over the cost of computing individual features. If there are NaN_{a} distinct chemical species in the system, this number is further multiplied by NaN_{a}. Hence, to reduce the computational cost of the already expensive long-range part, it is essential to make sure that the relevant long-range information is concentrated in as few coefficients as possible. It was shown previously that the original method proposed in 1 is not doing this efficiently.

To guide the following discussion, we will use nmax=6n_{\mathrm{max}}=6 and ℓmax=4\ell_{\mathrm{max}}=4 as an example, for which we obtain nmax⋅(ℓmax+1)2=150n_{\mathrm{max}}\cdot(\ell_{\mathrm{max}}+1)^{2}=150 features. A visual representation of all those features is presented in Figure S1. Each of the 150150 blue boxes corresponds to one feature, i.e. one set of possible values (n,ℓ,m)(n,\ell,m), ordered according to the radial index nn in the horizontal and angular index ℓ\ell in the vertical direction. The number of boxes is proportional to the computational cost of evaluating the features, and we will now examine how much long-range information is actually contained in these.

S3.1.1 First Consequence: Most Features Contain No Long-Range Information

We begin our discussion with the Coulomb potential. The key mathematical tool for this entire discussion will be the multipole expansion theorem, which is discussed in detail in the supporting information of 2. The discussion here will however be much more high-level, meaning that it is not necessary to understand the mathematical details of the theorem. It is important to note, however, that the results have been derived using open boundary conditions (for a charge density present in the entire space 3 decaying sufficiently quickly to be more precise), and not for periodic boundary conditions.

The first consequence of the multipole expansion theorem is that the entire long-range information can be condensed into a single radial channel, e.g. into the coefficients where n=0n=0.

This is visually represented in Figure S2 for our working example: out of the 150 coefficients that we needed to compute, it turns out that only 2525 contain long-range information, while the remaining 125 or 56≈83%\frac{5}{6}\approx 83\% in fact contain no long-range information at all! What this means in more practical terms is that if we keep the position of all atoms within a cutoff, but move the atoms outside of the cutoff, all features for n>0n>0 will be invariant under this operation. The coefficients for n>0n>0 therefore only depend on the position of the interior atoms.

Since the computational cost to evaluate the LODE features (after performing the reciprocal-space part of the algorithm) is proportional to the number of coefficients, we are essentially wasting 56≈83%\frac{5}{6}\approx 83\% of computational cost to compute some numbers that are pure short-range descriptors, the only difference being that the implementation is using a much more sophisticated and expensive algorithm. Given that long-range features are usually combined with another implementation that provides short-range descriptors, we are essentially just wasting computational effort. For a general value of nmaxn_{\mathrm{max}}, the fraction of wasted computational effort is 1−1nmax1-\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{max}}}. Note that this discussion only applies to the Coulomb potential, while the more general case of a power-law potential is discussed later.

This provides us with a simple and immediate optimization: we can simply stop computing features for n>0n>0, and only focus on n=0n=0. This leads to an improvement of the computational cost by a factor of typical values of nmaxn_{\mathrm{max}}, which is on the order of 6∼126\sim 12 for many applications, and hence about an order of magnitude.

S3.1.2 Second Consequence: Short-Range Contamination

The second key deficit of the original LODE formulation, as well as many alternative approaches to long-range ML as we discussed in the main text, is the fact that even the slowly-decaying Coulomb potential is primarily determined by short-range contributions from immediate neighbors (see also fig. 2 in the main text). While this is fine if our goal is to learn an actual Coulomb potential, this makes the methods less suitable for more general long-range ML.

What this means for our working example of LODE with nmax=6n_{\mathrm{max}}=6 and ℓmax=4\ell_{\mathrm{max}}=4 is visually illustrated in S3. We had already identified the column for n=0n=0 as the only one containing long-range information, but even this is mostly just short-range information with a tiny bit of long-range on top. This means that in the original formulation (and implementation) of LODE 1, a user would have spent a large computational cost to evaluate 150 features, 125 of which contain exactly zero long-range information, while the remaining 25 are also mostly short-range information.

While a sufficiently complex neural network might in principle be able to extract some long-range contributions from the 25 features, this signal is hidden behind the much larger short-range contributions that act as noise, making it unrealistic for this to happen in realistic datasets.

As we also recommend in the main text, short-ranged models today are quite mature, and much more efficient at capturing short-range information. Furthermore, it is also this short-range part that contains the dominant part of interactions, with long-range parts being corrections. This is why we always recommend to use long-range features in combination with a short-range ML part. In particular, this means that the n=0n=0 components of the LODE features, which are mostly short-ranged with a tiny fraction of long-range information, are unlikely to improve model performance by any significant extent.

The only exceptions to this general guideline are toy systems that have been constructed specifically to be challenging for short-range models. The original papers mostly discussed such systems, but did not include more realistic target materials, which made it harder to realize that LODE was essentially just computing short-range features in a very expensive manner.

The solution to this problem is the subtraction of the interior contributions. This makes the potential “unphysical”, but leads to descriptors that only contain long-range information. This is analogous to the “purified” long-range descriptors, also called exterior potential features (EPFs) in this work.

Both of these issues have already been addressed in our previous work 2, and the suggested solutions been implemented.

S3.2 Further Mathematical Consequences: From Last Publication to Current One

The two mathematical consequences and possible optimizations obtained from the multipole expansion theorem discussed so far had already been addressed in our last publication 2. We now discuss further mathematical consequences from the theorem, which strongly influenced the direction taken in this work.

S3.2.1 Third Consequence: Not all coefficients are equal

So far, we have argued that only the LODE coefficients for n=0n=0 contain long-range information (consequence 1) and that even extracting this information requires a purification process (consequence 2, also discussed in the main text). At the end of these steps, we still have to compute for each pair (ℓ,m)(\ell,m), where ℓ=0,1,…,ℓmax\ell=0,1,\dots,\ell_{\mathrm{max}} and m∈{−ℓ,…,ℓ}m\in\{-\ell,\dots,\ell\}. The third consequence from the multipole expansion theorem is the fact that the “amount” of long-range information in each of those coefficients depends on ℓ\ell. Note that the discussion here is still restricted to the Coulomb potential, with the general case delegated to the last subsection.

Stated slightly more mathematically, the third consequence states that in a LODE coefficient corresponding to the indices (ℓ,m)(\ell,m), the contribution of an atom at a distance rr is proportional to

1r1+ℓ.\displaystyle\frac{1}{r^{1+\ell}}\,. (S59)

i.e. decaying faster for larger indices ℓ\ell. In particular, this reduces to 1/r1/r for ℓ=0\ell=0, which is not surprising given that we are working with the Coulomb potential to begin with. For ℓ=1\ell=1, the contribution of an atom decays as 1/r21/r^{2}. This is the same decay as the electric field, and we will shortly explain that this is not a coincidence (the three coefficients for ℓ=1\ell=1 basically are the components of the electric field). More generally, as we keep making ℓ\ell large, the atomic contributions start to decay faster and faster. In particular, using a large angular index of ℓ=8\ell=8 would lead to contributions decaying as 1/r91/r^{9}, which can hardly be characterized as long-range.

Figure S4contains a visual representation of this fact. The bluer the color, the more long-ranged the information in the coefficients. This tells us that if the goal is to have a multi-scale model that combines short- and long-range features, it will suffice to only use LODE coefficients of small ℓ\ell, e.g. only ℓ=0,1,2\ell=0,1,2.

S3.2.2 Fourth Consequence: Relations between LODE Features, Potentials and Electric Fields

The fourth consequence from the multipole expansion theorem is that in a certain limit (namely the one in which the cutoff radius rcut→0r_{\mathrm{cut}}\rightarrow 0), the LODE coefficient for ℓ=0\ell=0 (and hence m=0m=0) becomes equal to the electrostatic potential at the position of the center atom, while the three LODE coefficients for ℓ=1\ell=1 (and hence m={−1,0,1}m=\{-1,0,1\}) become equal to the three components of the electric field at the position of the center atom. Note that to be more precise, both “equalities” are only true up to a global prefactor which can be computed analytically, and depends on the choice of LODE basis functions.

This fourth consequence is consistent with our previous observation, that the contribution of an atom at a distance rr decays as 1/r1+ℓ1/r^{1+\ell}, as this leads to 1/r1/r for ℓ=0\ell=0 and 1/r21/r^{2} for ℓ=1\ell=1. Note that the electric field is just the first derivative (or gradient to be more precise) of the potential. Focusing just on the radial dependence, 1/r21/r^{2} is the first derivative of 1/r1/r with respect to rr up to a global prefactor of (−1)(-1).

More generally, the ℓ\ell-th derivative of 1/r1/r is 1/r1+ℓ1/r^{1+\ell} up to a prefactor, which is precisely the contribution of an atom to a LODE coefficient with index ℓ\ell. We might hence guess that more generally, the LODE components for some ℓ\ell are related to the ℓ\ell-th derivatives of the potential. This guess turns out to be correct, and can be proven using the connection between the spherical and Cartesian versions of the multipole expansion.

Thus, if implemented using an autodifferentiable framework such as PyTorch or JAX, one can in principle obtain all LODE coefficients just from the EPFs via suitable differentiation.

In other words, it suffices to implement the EPFs (the ℓ=0\ell=0 part), which will automatically provide us with the components for ℓ=1\ell=1 by taking a single differentiation step, ℓ=2\ell=2 by using second derivatives etc. This procedure clearly becomes less and less efficient for larger ℓ\ell, but shows that in principle, our framework is fully able to generate the LODE features without too much extra effort. The main text also discusses some additional capabilities that have been added to also compute the features for higher angular indices ℓ\ell efficiently.

Despite of this possibility, we do not recommend to use higher-ℓ\ell coefficients too extensively. This is due to the previous observation that the larger ℓ\ell becomes, the faster the contributions of the far-away atoms decay. This is why in this work, we suggest alternative methods to extract long-range information more efficiently: by modifying the particle weights (or charges) qiq_{i} and the interaction exponent pp. The next subsection discusses how some of the results discussed so far change when moving to a more general exponent pp.

S3.3 Mathematical Results for General Exponents pp

The results so far have exclusively been about the Coulomb potential, which is the most important long-range interaction. Both the LODE features and the EPFs introduced in this work can however easily be generalized to arbitrary 1/rp1/r^{p} inverse power-law potentials with p>0p>0 being a positive real number.

As discussed extensively in the supporting information of our previous work 2, the multipole expansion theorem for this general case is quite different from the Coulomb potential, which is the special case for p=1p=1. It might at first seem surprising that among all positive reals, the Coulomb potential only is very different. We thus explain this first in the next subsection. Readers only interested in the consequences for ML models can skip directly to the final part.

S3.3.1 Generalized Multipole Expansion

The special nature of the Coulomb potential v⁡(r)=1/rv(r)=1/r arises from the fact that it is a solution to the Laplace equation

Δ​v=∇2v=0\displaystyle\Delta v=\nabla^{2}v=0 (S60)

for r≠0r\neq 0, where Δ=∇2\Delta=\nabla^{2} is the Laplace-operator. In fact, it is the unique spherically symmetric solution to this equation apart from the constant function! This defining property of the Coulomb potential, perhaps surprisingly, has a dramatic impact on its multipole expansion.

Remembering the definition of the Laplace operator, this means that a certain linear combination of second derivatives of vv vanishes. If we perform a Taylor expansion (in three dimensions) of a generic smooth function vv, the quadratic term consists of 66 independent terms proportional to x2,y2,z2,x​y,x​z,y​zx^{2},y^{2},z^{2},xy,xz,yz respectively (since x​y=y​xxy=yx commute, as do the derivatives). The prefactors of these terms are precisely the six second derivatives of the target function with respect to two of the three variables. If a function vv is a solution to the Laplace equation, however, this means that a linear combination of these six second derivatives is zero, and hence that only five of the derivatives are actually independent. This is why for the Coulomb potential, the contributions with ℓ=2\ell=2 decaying as 1/r1+ℓ=1/r31/r^{1+\ell}=1/r^{3} only contain five terms: m∈{−2,−1,0,1,2}m\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}. The pattern of vanishing derivatives propagates to higher-order derivatives, which means that for the ℓ\ell-th derivatives, only 2​ℓ+12\ell+1 are independent. This is what makes the Coulomb potential so special when it comes to its Taylor expansion.

For a more generic function, i.e. a function that is not a solution of the Laplace equation, there are no such cancellations, and in general at order ℓ\ell, there ar

(ℓ+22)=(ℓ+2)​(ℓ+1)2∼ℓ2\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\ell+2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}=\frac{(\ell+2)(\ell+1)}{2}\sim\ell^{2} (S61)

independent terms in its Taylor expansion. This Taylor expansion is also called “Cartesian multipole expansion”, as all the terms of ℓ\ell-th derivatives decay as 1/r1+ℓ1/r^{1+\ell} (with some angular dependence), just as for the usual or “spherical” multipole expansion.

So far, we have explained how the Taylor or Cartesian multipole expansion of a generic 1/rp1/r^{p} potential contains a lot more terms than 1/r1/r. The final step to fully make the connection to the LODE coefficients is to connect this Cartesian multipole expansion to the usual “spherical” multipole expansion. This last step simply requires the realization that a spherical harmonic function YℓmY_{\ell}^{m} is, up to a factor of rℓr^{\ell}, just a polynomial of degree ℓ\ell in the Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z)(x,y,z). Hence, going from the Cartesian coordinates to spherical harmonics is simply a linear change of basis, which shows that both the Cartesian and spherical multipole expansions are equivalent term-by-term up to a change of basis. The more explicit statements are discussed in the next subsection.

S3.3.2 Fifth consequence: Results are More Complicated But Similar for General Inverse Power-Law Potential

For LODE features generated from a general 1/rp1/r^{p} inverse power-law potential with p≠1p\neq 1, the information content in the LODE coefficients behaves differently from the Coulomb potential. The generalized multipole expansion discussed in the supporting information in our previous work 2 shows that it is not possible to condense the entire long-range information into n=0n=0, and that all values of nn are relevant. Hence, there are now relevant LODE coefficients for all values of the indices (ℓ,m,n)(\ell,m,n) rather than just (ℓ,m)(\ell,m).

For a given coefficient, the contribution of an atom at a distance of rr from the center then decays as

1rp+ℓ+2​n.\displaystyle\frac{1}{r^{p+\ell+2n}}\,. (S62)

This shows more directly that all radial channels nn are important, but also that the decay is much faster for large nn. Hence, the general trends are still similar to the Coulomb potential: The majority of the long-range information is contained in the coefficients with n=0n=0 and small values of ℓ\ell such as ℓ=0,1,2\ell=0,1,2. The only difference is that now, also the coefficients with n=1,2n=1,2 contain some long-range information. This is visualized in Figure S5.

The relation between the potential (or EPFs) and the analogue of the electric field are the same as for the Coulomb potential. The LODE coefficient for n=0n=0 and ℓ=0\ell=0 still corresponds to the potential (or EPF) at the location of the center atom. Furthermore, the three “generalized electric field” coefficients with n=0n=0 and ℓ=1\ell=1 (and hence m∈{−1,0,1}m\in\{-1,0,1\}) by taking the gradient of the coefficient with n=0n=0 and ℓ=0\ell=0.

Despite of this more complicated nature, these facts and the fast decay with respect to nn means that the conclusions are mostly similar to the Coulomb potential. This is why instead of building expensive LODE features by using multiple values of ℓ\ell and nn, we suggest to just use the potential itself (which essentially corresponds to LODE with n=ℓ=m=0n=\ell=m=0) with different charges and the option to add gradients (essentially adding the coefficients for ℓ=1\ell=1) either using the full or exterior variant.

S4 Tuning the Ewald and PME parameters

In the following, we discuss the procedure we implement to tune the optimal parameters, by minimizing the absolute force error estimation. We define the total force error as

Δ​F\displaystyle\Delta F =Δ​FSR2+Δ​FLR2\displaystyle=\sqrt{\Delta F_{\mathrm{SR}}^{2}+\Delta F_{\mathrm{LR}}^{2}}\, (S63)

where Δ​FSR\Delta F_{\mathrm{SR}} and Δ​FLR\Delta F_{\mathrm{LR}} are the absolute real-space and Fourier-domain errors. Giving expressions for the expected error of general structures is difficult and usual error estimations assume homogenous random systems.

For all methods the real space error is3

ΔFSR≈Q2N2rcut​Ve−rcut2/2σ2\displaystyle\Delta F_{\mathrm{SR}}\approx\frac{Q^{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\frac{2}{\sqrt{r_{\text{cut}}V}}e^{-r_{\text{cut}}^{2}/2\sigma^{2}} (S64)

where NN is the number of charges, Q2=∑i=1Nqi2Q^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_{i}^{2}, is the sum of squared charges, and VV is the volume of the system.

For Ewald, the approximate force error is3, 4

ΔFLREwald≈Q2N2/σπ​2​V/he−2π2σ2/h2\displaystyle\Delta F_{\mathrm{LR}}^{\mathrm{Ewald}}\approx\frac{Q^{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\frac{\sqrt{2}/\sigma}{\pi\sqrt{2V/h}}e^{-2\pi^{2}\sigma^{2}/h^{2}} (S65)

For PME it reads 5

Δ​FLRPME≈2​π1/4​3​2/σN⁡(2​P+3)​Q2L2​(2​H/σ)P+1(P+1)!×exp⁡(P+1)​[log⁡(P+1)−log⁡2−1]2​⟨ϕP2⟩1/2\displaystyle\Delta F_{\mathrm{LR}}^{\mathrm{PME}}\approx 2\pi^{1/4}\sqrt{\frac{3\sqrt{2}/\sigma}{N(2P+3)}}\frac{Q^{2}}{L^{2}}\frac{(\sqrt{2}H/\sigma)^{P+1}}{(P+1)!}\times\exp{\frac{(P+1)[\log{(P+1)}-\log 2-1]}{2}}\left<\phi_{P}^{2}\right>^{1/2} (S66)

where PP is the order of the interpolation scheme, HH is the spacing of mesh points, and ϕP2=H−(P+1)​∏s∈SH(P)(x−s)\phi_{P}^{2}=H^{-(P+1)}\prod_{s\in S_{H}^{(P)}}(x-s), in which SH(P)S_{H}^{(P)} is the P+1P+1 mesh points closest to the point xx.

For P3M the error is6

Δ​FLRP3M\displaystyle\Delta F_{\mathrm{LR}}^{\mathrm{P3M}} ≈Q2L2​(2​Hσ)P​2​LN​σ​2​π​∑m=0P−1am(P)​(2​Hσ)2​m\displaystyle\approx\frac{Q^{2}}{L^{2}}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}H}{\sigma}\right)^{P}\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{2}L}{N\sigma}\sqrt{2\pi}\sum_{m=0}^{P-1}a_{m}^{(P)}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}H}{\sigma}\right)^{2m}} (S67)

where am(P)a_{m}^{(P)} is an expansion coefficient, and its exact value can be found in Table II in Ref. 6.

Based on the error formulas above, and for a given trial structure that is representative of those most commonly used for the problem at hand, we can tune the parameters to achieve the desired accuracy following the algorithm below.

  • Step 1

    Based on the user given accuracy ϵtarget\epsilon_{\mathrm{target}} and rcutr_{\mathrm{cut}}, calculate the smearing σ\sigma by solving Δ​FSR​(σ,rcut)=ϵtarget/2\Delta F_{\mathrm{SR}}(\sigma;r_{\mathrm{cut}})=\epsilon_{\mathrm{target}}/2.

  • Step 2

    Initialize sets of kk-space parameters. For Ewald, the values are chosen such that each spatial direction (x, y, z) contains between 1 and 13 mesh points. For mesh-based methods (P3M and PME), the grid sizes range from 2 to 7 mesh points per spatial direction, considering all possible interpolation orders.

  • Step 3

    Evaluate all possible parameter sets. The error associated with the parameter is estimated cheaply using the error formulas. Parameters that yield error within the desired accuracy are benchmarked estimating the empirical timings for an evaluation of energy and derivatives. Parameter sets exceeding the error threshold are not tested for performance and their timings are set as infinity.

  • Step 4

    Return the parameter set achieving the desired accuracy with the shortest timing. If no parameter set can fulfill the accuracy requirement, the set achieving the smallest error is returned.

In Figure S6 we show the results of the tuning procedure for Ewald, PME, and P3M similarly to Figure 3 in the main text but for double precision (64-bit) floating point numbers. As already described we find also that we achieve the requested accuracy for the Madelung constants but the accuracy saturates around 10−410^{-4} for Ewald summation and 10−510^{-5} for the mesh calculators.

In figure Figure S7 we show the optimal parameters for Ewald summation which leads to a scaling proportional to N3/2N^{3/2} together with the quadratic scaling as it is shown in the main text in Figure 4A. The optimal scaling was achieved by setting

smearing\displaystyle\mathrm{smearing} =1.3⋅N1/6/2\displaystyle=1.3\cdot N^{1/6}/\sqrt{2}
lr​_​wavelength\displaystyle\mathrm{lr\_wavelength} =2​π⋅smearing/2.2\displaystyle=2\pi\cdot\mathrm{smearing}/2.2 (S68)
rc\displaystyle\mathrm{r_{c}} =2.2⋅smearing\displaystyle=2.2\cdot\mathrm{smearing}

The parameters and pre-factors were obtained from systematic tests on a CsCl\mathrm{CsCl} system, where the unit cell is replicated 16 times along each spatial dimension, yielding a total system of 8192 atoms.

S5 Finding the optimal cutoff for benchmarking

To find the optimal cutoff for our benchmark simulations we perform a grid search over the real space cutoff for a replicated NaCl structure in a cubic cell. We replicated the initial cell 32 in each direction leading to a total of 262144 atoms in a cell with a side length of 64 Å. We use the same LAMMPS P3M setup as in the main text, but we only vary the real-space cutoff. Figure S8 shows the time per step versus the real space cutoff, showing the optimum efficiency is achieved for a value of 4.44.4 Å.

S6 GPU Utilization

During the benchmarks discussed in section IV A of the main text, we collected statistics on GPU utilization (the percentage of time during which at least one kernel is executed) and power draw (power consumed by the GPU) to estimate the extent to which our code, as well as the LAMMPS reference implementation, can make use of the available hardware. The results are shown in Figure S9.

At system sizes below approximately 1000010000 atoms, the GPU is not fully utilized. Even at large sizes, neither our code nor LAMMPS is able to fully exhaust the available hardware, as shown by the power draw not reaching the peak design capacity of 700700 W. Therefore, we expect that significant further performance improvements can be achieved by more specifically targetting specific GPUs, for instance by overlapping memory access and compute, reducing overhead, and making use of reduced-precision operations where appropriate.

S7 MD of Water at constant energy and volume

Similar to the main text shown in Figure 5, we perform MD simulations of the water system without thermostats at constant energy and volume (NVE) over 20​ps20\,\mathrm{ps} using the same settings as described in section IV B of the main text. Figure S10 shows the temperature and the energy of the system. We perform two simulations: in one, we compute the Coulomb energy in single precision (32-bit floating-point numbers), and in the other, we use double precision. In both cases, the energy is conserved, verifying that the forces are the exact derivative of the energy up to numerical precision.
